Those living in cities that dimmed their streetlights were less likely to be deterred from venturing out at night and were also less likely to be affected in their choice of transportation. Respondents in both cities that dim and do not dim largely agreed that dimmed streetlights reduce light pollution, save energy, and reduce glare. The opinions of residents in dimming cities and non-dimming cities were mixed on whether dimmed streetlights affect their ability to see at night and whether dimmed streetlights pose a security risk at night. 4.3 Energy Considerations The impact of the adaptive lighting on energy consumption is found in two ways. The first is the reduction in the initial lighting to 70% of full brightness, which accounts for a clean new luminaire that will get dirty over time and the output will be reduced with age. To overcome this loss, the power on the luminaire will be increased, meaning that at end of the life the luminaire will be operating at full power to account for the predicted losses due to dirt and degradation of the light source. The second source of energy consumption reduction is the dimming of the luminaires by time of day. As discussed, this dimming occurs at 8:00 p.m. for the C3 roads, 10:00 p.m. for C2, and finally midnight for the C1 roads. Using these times, and the sunrise and sunset time for the City of Cambridge, the impact on energy for the adaptive lighting system can be calculated. These results are shown for both new luminaires and luminaries at the end of life. The sunrise and sunset times were selected based on the first day of each month. Note that the chart shows the percentage of usage, not the percentage of savings. The savings can be calculated at 100% minus the values shown in the chart. The calculation shows that the savings that result from the dimming system vary by month and by the roadway type. With the C3 roadways being dimmed for the longest period of time, the energy reduction is more significant than the other roadway types.
